title: Millbrae
name: Millbrae
metaTitle: 1031 Exchange Millbrae CA | 1031 Exchange San Francisco
metaDescription: Millbrae 1031 exchange coordination for transit-adjacent multifamily, small hotel, and Broadway retail owners near the BART and Caltrain hub.

sections.html: Millbrae is small, but the intermodal station at its center, one of the few spots on the Peninsula where BART and Caltrain actually meet, has reshaped what gets built and bought around it. I have coordinated closings here where the biggest scheduling constraint wasn't the buyer or seller, it was getting a construction crew access next to an active rail platform. That single fact changes how a facilities manager thinks about almost every capital project within a few blocks of the station.

sections.heading: A Small City Defined by Two Rail Lines
sections.html:
Millbrae's investment stock is compact, and most of it falls into a few clear categories:

  • Newer transit-oriented multifamily and mixed-use development near the station
  • Smaller branded hotels serving SFO travelers
  • Neighborhood retail along Broadway
  • Older multifamily buildings on the residential side of the city
  • Limited office space serving local professional tenants

The newer transit-oriented buildings tend to have denser parking structures and more shared amenity space than the older residential stock further from the station, which changes both the operating budget and the tenant expectations a new owner should plan around.

sections.heading: Identifying Replacements in a Small, Specific Market
sections.html: Because Millbrae's newer transit-oriented product is limited in supply, a seller exiting one of those buildings often needs the 200% rule to widen the search into comparable development elsewhere on the Peninsula. A seller trading a smaller hotel or Broadway retail asset can usually stay with the three-property rule if the search stays close by. I encourage sellers to finalize that list with their qualified intermediary well ahead of the 45-day deadline, since a small market like this one can move quickly once a good candidate comes up.

sections.heading: The Downtime That Comes From Building Next to Active Rail
sections.html: Any construction or major mechanical work near the station has to work around BART and Caltrain's own operating windows, which means night or weekend access more often than a standard weekday schedule, and that changes how long a renovation actually takes. I always ask for the transit agency coordination history on a property before assuming a buyer's planned upgrade will move as fast as it would somewhere without a rail platform next door. Crane placement and material staging near the platforms often require their own agency sign-off, and that approval process can add weeks to a project timeline that would otherwise be routine.

sections.heading: Coordinating Closing Around a Compressed Timeline
sections.html: Smaller deals here can move quickly, which is an advantage, but it also means the qualified intermediary, lender, and title company need to stay ahead of the 45-day identification window rather than assuming a simple property means simple timing. Rail-adjacent construction permits in particular can take longer to pull than the rest of the closing process, so I raise that question before the identification deadline, not after. A buyer with a renovation planned right after closing should have that agency conversation started during due diligence, not saved for after the deed records.

sections.heading: What Works for Millbrae Investors
sections.html: The buyers who do well here account for the rail line as a real operational constraint on any construction plan, rather than treating proximity to the station as only a leasing advantage. That same proximity that draws tenants in also shapes every contractor's bid, and pricing in that reality upfront avoids an unpleasant renegotiation later. It's a small enough market that word travels fast among the handful of contractors who regularly work near the station, so a buyer's reputation with them matters more here than in a larger city.

faqs.q: Does being near the Millbrae intermodal station actually slow down construction work?
faqs.a: It can, since work adjacent to active BART and Caltrain infrastructure often requires coordination with those agencies and may be restricted to certain hours. That constraint is worth factoring into any post-closing renovation timeline. A contractor with prior experience working near this specific station is often worth the extra cost given how much smoother that coordination tends to go.

faqs.q: How many replacement properties should I identify if I'm exiting transit-oriented development here?
faqs.a: More than three is common, since comparable newer development directly in Millbrae is limited. The 200% rule allows a seller to widen the list to similar Peninsula transit-adjacent product, whether that's in nearby San Bruno, Burlingame, or another BART or Caltrain corridor.

faqs.q: Is a small hotel near SFO a realistic 1031 replacement for multifamily?
faqs.a: It can be for an investor comfortable with a different management and revenue model, since hotel income depends on occupancy and rate performance rather than a signed lease. That difference deserves its own diligence conversation, and a smaller hotel here often runs on a leaner staffing model than a larger branded property closer to the airport itself, which changes both the risk profile and the day-to-day facilities workload a new owner should expect to take on.

faqs.q: What should a buyer check before closing on Broadway retail in Millbrae?
faqs.a: Lease term, parking availability, and the surrounding tenant mix all matter on a small commercial strip like this, since foot traffic depends on the block staying active rather than any single anchor tenant. A quick walk of the block at different times of day tells you more about actual foot traffic than any leasing brochure will.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange San Francisco confirm my Millbrae property qualifies as an exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification, scheduling, and communication among the investor's advisors. Whether a specific property and transaction qualify is a determination made by the investor's CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary, particularly where rail-adjacent construction plans affect the timeline.
